title: TotalView-ITCH 5.0
text: Every displayed order on Nasdaq, every change to it, and every execution arrives as a small binary message. That stream is TotalView-ITCH 5.0. Let's read it one message at a time.

title: Events, not a book
text: ITCH does not send you a book. It sends the events that build one. Each add, execute, cancel and delete names one order by its reference number. Your feed handler applies them in order, and the book is what they leave behind. Nasdaq sends the stream over MoldUDP64 multicast, or over SoupBinTCP. The next two videos cover those.

title: The 11-byte header
text: Every message starts with the same eleven bytes. One byte of message type, an ASCII letter. Two bytes of stock locate, a small number for the instrument, assigned fresh each day starting at one. Two bytes of tracking number, for Nasdaq's internal use. Then six bytes of timestamp: nanoseconds since midnight. All integers are big-endian.

title: Add Order: 36 bytes
text: An order enters the book with Add Order, type A, thirty six bytes. After the header comes an eight byte order reference, unique for the day. One byte of side, B or S. Four bytes of shares. Eight bytes of symbol, padded with spaces. And four bytes of price: an integer with four implied decimals. Type F is the same message, plus a four byte market participant ID.

title: An order's life
text: After that, messages name the order only by its reference. E, order executed, carries shares and a match number. X cancels some of the shares. U replaces the order with a new reference, size and price. D deletes what is left. And P reports trades against hidden orders that were never on the book.

title: Worked example
text: Here is an illustrative add at the open. The timestamp is thirty four point two trillion nanoseconds: 9:30 exactly. Reference 1234, buy, 100 shares of AAPL. The price bytes are hex 1C E0 94, or 1,892,500, so 189.25 dollars. An execution of 40 shares leaves 60. A cancel of 10 leaves 50. A delete removes the rest.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's codec writes each message once, as a list of field offsets. The same list drives decode and encode, so the two cannot drift apart. A compile-time check fails the build if the list does not end at the spec length. And itch-dump replays a whole day into the book builder, which must report zero integrity errors.

title: Pitfalls
text: Four traps catch new feed handlers. Nasdaq may append fields, so accept longer messages and ignore the extra bytes. An order executed down to zero is dead: remove it without waiting for a delete. Locate codes change daily, so map them from the stock directory. And keep prices as integers, never floats. ITCH is a log of order events; the book is yours to build.
